                                                         Defendant.
                                  11

                                  12            Plaintiff PVC Fence Wholesale, LLC is a company that purchases online advertisements
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   from defendant Google LLC through the Google Ads program. PVC Fence filed this putative class

                                  14   action to challenge “Google’s unlawful practice of charging its customers for alleged advertising”

                                  15   without providing sufficient “information supporting or justifying the charges” (i.e., without

                                  16   always specifying the context in which Google displayed the advertisements). Google now moves

                                  17   to strike PVC Fence’s first amended complaint, to compel arbitration of PVC Fence’s claims, and,

                                  18   in the alternative, to dismiss PVC Fence’s first amended complaint. For the reasons below, the

                                  19   Court denies the motion to strike, grants the motion to compel arbitration, and denies the motion

                                  20   to dismiss based on the parties’ agreement to submit such issues to the arbitrator rather than the

                                  21   Court.

                                  22                                            BACKGROUND

                                  23            This action concerns Google’s online advertising program: Google Ads. Through that

                                  24   program, customers can bid to place targeted advertisements on Google’s search engine in

                                  25   response to specific queries submitted by users. Customers pay on a “per click” basis—that is,

                                  26   Google charges customers a fee only if a user actually clicks on the advertisement. PVC Fence, a

                                  27   Florida-based company, is a Google Ads customer that uses the program to advertise its fencing

                                  28   materials for sale.
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP            Document 46          Filed 03/16/26     Page 2 of 10




                                   1          Google requires all Google Ads customers to agree to certain terms. In September 2017,

                                   2   Google added an arbitration provision to those terms, requiring binding individual arbitration of

                                   3   “all disputes and claims between Google and [the] Customer” that “arise out of or relate in any

                                   4   way to the [Ads] Program or [Ads] Terms.” The arbitration provision also included a “30-day opt-

                                   5   out period,” allowing customers to opt out of the arbitration provision by “notify[ing] Google”

                                   6   through a hyperlinked webform “within 30 days of the first acceptance date of any version of the[]

                                   7   Terms containing an arbitration provision.” In addition to containing an arbitration provision in

                                   8   the body of the terms, the September 2017 terms included a notice in the first paragraph that

                                   9   the new terms “require the use of binding individual arbitration to resolve disputes rather than jury

                                  10   trials or class actions.” The first paragraph also instructed customers that they “may opt out of the

                                  11   requirement to arbitrate disputes by following the instructions in [the relevant section] within 30

                                  12   days of the first acceptance date of any version of these Terms containing an arbitration
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   provision.”

                                  14          PVC Fence first created a Google Ads account in 2011, before the arbitration provision

                                  15   was implemented in September 2017. According to the declaration of Armete Mobin, a legal

                                  16   specialist on the Google Ads legal team, Google provided notice of the new arbitration provision

                                  17   to such pre-existing Google Ads customers through (1) a public blog post in August 2017, (2)

                                  18   direct emails to Google Ads customers, and (3) “an alert displayed to advertisers when they logged

                                  19   into their accounts.” “Each of these notices contained the same or substantially similar language”

                                  20   and explained that Google was “rolling out new Terms and Conditions” including, “[i]n the U.S.

                                  21   … a provision to use arbitration to resolve disputes rather than jury trials or class actions.” The

                                  22   notices instructed customers that they could “[f]ollow the instructions in the dispute resolution

                                  23   section of the terms to opt-out of this provision.” The notices then provided a link to “review and

                                  24   accept” the new terms. Upon clicking the link, customers were taken to a page with the full terms

                                  25   in a scroll-box, where they were prompted to accept or reject the September 2017 terms. At the top

                                  26   of the page was another notice asking customers to “[p]lease review these terms carefully” as

                                  27   “[t]hey include the use of binding arbitration to resolve disputes rather than jury trials or class

                                  28   actions.” The notice told customers to “follow the instructions in the terms below if you wish to
                                                                                          2
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP            Document 46          Filed 03/16/26     Page 3 of 10




                                   1   opt out of this provision.” In addition to providing opt-out information in the body of the terms,

                                   2   the notice at the top of the page also included a hyperlink labelled “Learn more,” which linked to

                                   3   the webform to opt out of the arbitration provision.

                                   4           “Google’s records reflect that [PVC Fence] accepted the September 2017 Terms,”

                                   5   including the arbitration provision, “on October 25, 2017.” And Google’s records “do not reflect

                                   6   any attempts by … PVC Fence[] to opt out of the Arbitration Provision.” Ms. Mobin attested that,

                                   7   after accepting the arbitration provision, “PVC Fence continued to purchase advertising on the

                                   8   Google Ads platform.”

                                   9          PVC Fence filed this action against Google in 2025. Its operative first amended complaint

                                  10   alleges that Google falsely promises Google Ads customers that they may control the specific

                                  11   search parameters in response to which their advertisements will be displayed. According to PVC

                                  12   Fence, Google in fact occludes many of the queries in response to which advertisements are
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   displayed, preventing customers like PVC Fence from exercising full control.

                                  14          On behalf of a putative class of Google Ads customers, PVC Fence asserts claims for

                                  15   (1) breach of contract; (2) breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing; (3) quasi-contract;

                                  16   (4) false advertising in violation of California’s False Advertising Law (FAL), Cal. Bus. & Prof.

                                  17   Code § 17500; (5) violation of California’s Unfair Competition Law, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code

                                  18   § 17200; and (6) a declaratory judgment. PVC Fence seeks monetary relief in the form of

                                  19   damages, restitution, and reasonable attorney’s fees. It also seeks injunctive relief ordering Google

                                  20   to “cease and desist from publishing false, deceptive, and misleading marketing statements related

                                  21   to the Google Ads product and service”; “cease refusing to provide to [PVC Fence] and all current

                                  22   and future Google Ads users necessary information concerning the ‘Other Search Term’”; and

                                  23   “cease making false claims in its advertising promulgated towards Google Ads users and potential

                                  24   users concerning the information it provides.” Finally, PVC Fence seeks a declaration that

                                  25   Google’s challenged practices are unlawful and that various provisions in the Google Ads terms

                                  26   are unenforceable.

                                  27          Now before the Court is Google’s motion to strike the first amended complaint, to compel

                                  28   arbitration of this action, and, in the alternative, to dismiss the first amended complaint.
                                                                                          3

                                   1                                           LEGAL STANDARD

                                   2          The Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) provides that a “written provision in ... a contract

                                   3   evidencing a transaction involving commerce to settle by arbitration a controversy thereafter

                                   4   arising out of such contract or transaction ... shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon

                                   5   such grounds as exist at law or in equity for the revocation of any contract.” 9 U.S.C. § 2. As this

                                   6   language makes clear, “an arbitration agreement is a contract like any other.” Bielski v. Coinbase,

                                   7   Inc., 87 F.4th 1003, 1009 (9th Cir. 2023). The FAA “requires courts to rigorously enforce

                                   8   agreements to arbitrate.” Johnson v. Walmart, Inc., 57 F.4th 677, 681 (9th Cir. 2023).

                                   9          In deciding a motion to compel arbitration, a court must determine “(1) whether a valid

                                  10   agreement to arbitrate exists and, if it does, (2) whether the agreement encompasses the dispute at

                                  11   issue.” Chiron Corp. v. Ortho Diagnostic Sys. Inc., 207 F.3d 1126, 1130 (9th Cir. 2000). But even

                                  12   if the answer to both questions is yes, the arbitration may be subject to “generally applicable
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   contract defenses” like “fraud, duress, or unconscionability.” Lim v. TForce Logs., LLC, 8 F.4th

                                  14   992, 999 (9th Cir. 2021). In determining whether a valid and enforceable arbitration agreement

                                  15   encompasses the parties’ dispute, the Court applies the summary-judgment standard. Hansen v.

                                  16   LMB Mortg. Servs., Inc., 1 F.4th 667, 670 (9th Cir. 2021). Thus, if the Court determines that a

                                  17   genuine dispute of material fact exists as to existence or enforceability of an agreement to arbitrate

                                  18   a plaintiff’s claims, that arbitrability dispute generally must proceed to trial. See 9 U.S.C. § 4.

                                  19                                                ANALYSIS

                                  20   I.     Google’s motion to strike the first amended complaint is denied.
                                  21          After Google moved to dismiss PVC Fence’s original complaint, the parties stipulated to

                                  22   an extension of PVC Fence’s deadline to file an “opposition” to that motion. But rather than file

                                  23   an opposition, PVC Fence filed its first amended complaint. Google therefore moves to strike the

                                  24   first amended complaint as untimely.

                                  25          PVC Fence concedes that the parties’ stipulation did not expressly permit it to file the first

                                  26   amended complaint and that it filed the first amended complaint after the deadline for amendment

                                  27   as a matter of course under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a). But PVC Fence asks the Court

                                  28   to grant an extension of time nunc pro tunc because its failure either to seek leave to amend or to
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP           Document 46         Filed 03/16/26      Page 5 of 10




                                   1   secure a stipulation authorizing its belated amendment was mistaken. See Hayes v. District of

                                   2   Columbia, 275 F.R.D. 343, 346 (D.D.C. 2011).

                                   3          Given the liberal amendment policy embodied in the federal rules and “[i]n the interest of

                                   4   efficient judicial administration,” see id., the Court grants PVC Fence’s requested nunc pro tunc

                                   5   extension. The Court therefore denies Google’s motion to strike the first amended complaint.

                                   6   II.    Google’s motion to compel arbitration is granted.
                                   7          Google asserts that PVC Fence’s claims are subject to the arbitration provision added to

                                   8   the Google Ads terms in September 2017. PVC Fence does not dispute that it agreed to the

                                   9   arbitration provision and that the provision covers this dispute. Instead, PVC Fence argues that the

                                  10   arbitration provision is unenforceable on two grounds. First, PVC Fence argues that the

                                  11   arbitration provision is unconscionable. Second, it argues that the provision invalidly prohibits it

                                  12   from pursuing claims for public injunctive relief. Both arguments fail.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13          A.      The arbitration provision is not unconscionable.
                                  14          PVC Fence contends that the arbitration provision is unconscionable. In California, “[a]

                                  15   contract is unconscionable if one of the parties lacked a meaningful choice in deciding whether to

                                  16   agree and the contract contains terms that are unreasonably favorable to the other party.” OTO,

                                  17   L.L.C. v. Kho, 8 Cal. 5th 111, 125 (2019). Unconscionability includes both “a procedural and a

                                  18   substantive element.” Id. The procedural element addresses the process by which the parties

                                  19   formed the contract and the substantive element addresses the fairness of the contract’s

                                  20   terms. Id. “[P]rocedural and substantive unconscionability must both be present in order for a

                                  21   court ... to refuse to enforce a contract or clause,” but “they need not be present in the same

                                  22   degree.” Armendariz v. Found. Health Psychcare Servs., Inc., 24 Cal. 4th 83, 114 (2000) (citation

                                  23   modified).

                                  24          Whether or not the arbitration provision is substantively unconscionable, PVC Fence has

                                  25   offered no evidence that it is procedurally unconscionable. PVC Fence’s procedural

                                  26   unconscionability argument boils down to a contention that the September 2017 terms are an

                                  27   adhesive contract that PVC Fence had no opportunity to negotiate. But as detailed above, Google

                                  28   has presented evidence that the arbitration provision contained an unambiguous opt-out provision
                                                                                         5
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP            Document 46          Filed 03/16/26     Page 6 of 10




                                   1   allowing PVC Fence to decline the arbitration provision within 30 days of entering into the

                                   2   contract with Google. This Court has already explained that such an opt-out provision in Google’s

                                   3   terms defeats any argument that an arbitration agreement is adhesive. See Cal. Crane Sch., Inc. v.

                                   4   Google LLC (“Crane III”), 722 F. Supp. 3d 1026, 1034 (N.D. Cal. 2024), aff’d, No. 24-4604, 2025

                                   5   WL 2541913 (9th Cir. Sept. 4, 2025); see also Cal. Crane Sch., Inc. v. Google LLC (“Crane I”),

                                   6   621 F. Supp. 3d 1024, 1030 (N.D. Cal. 2022); Trudeau v. Google LLC, 349 F. Supp. 3d 869, 877

                                   7   (N.D. Cal. 2018) (“This Court finds that the 2017 [Terms] provided a meaningful opportunity to

                                   8   opt out of the arbitration provision.”), aff’d, 816 F. App’x 68 (9th Cir. 2020).

                                   9          PVC Fence’s argument that the arbitration provision is adhesive notwithstanding the opt-

                                  10   out provision is unavailing.

                                  11          First, PVC Fence insists that Google’s “monopoly over online search advertising leaves

                                  12   advertisers” like PVC Fence “with no viable alternatives” and “effectively eviscerates any
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   negotiating power advertisers may have.” But as this Court has previously stated:

                                  14                  Google’s opt-out provision … undercuts [PVC Fence]’s position that
                                                      Google had overwhelming bargaining power with respect to the
                                  15                  arbitration agreement. In contrast to an unconscionable take-it-or-
                                                      leave-it contract, the arbitration agreement here allowed a customer
                                  16                  to take-it, opt-out-of-arbitration-and-then-take-it, or leave-it. Even if
                                  17                  other terms of Google’s Terms of Service were found to be adhesive,
                                                      the same cannot be said of the Terms’ arbitration provisions, which
                                  18                  the Court must consider separate and apart from the remainder of the
                                                      contract. See Buckeye Check Cashing, Inc. v. Cardegna, 546 U.S.
                                  19                  440, 445 (2006) (“[A]s a matter of substantive federal arbitration law,
                                                      an arbitration provision is severable from the remainder of the
                                  20                  contract.”).
                                  21   Crane III, 722 F. Supp. 3d at 1034–35.
                                  22          Second, PVC Fence argues that “even if an agreement is not adhesive, it can still be found

                                  23   sufficiently surprise-laden or oppressive to implicate procedural unconscionability.” See Rios v.

                                  24   HRB Digital LLC, No. 25-cv-03530, 2025 WL 3003768, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 27, 2025). That

                                  25   may be true in some cases, such as where a defendant exerts pressure on a plaintiff not to exercise

                                  26   a right to opt out or where the opt out option is illusory. See id. at *8 (collecting such cases).

                                  27   In Rios, for example, another court in this district found that an arbitration agreement with an opt-

                                  28   out provision was unconscionable, though not adhesive, because the opt-out provision required
                                                                                          6
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP               Document 46       Filed 03/16/26    Page 7 of 10




                                   1   consumers to “submit a new opt-out request each year” such that “even users who once opted out

                                   2   may be swept back into arbitration unless they repeatedly navigate the process annually.” Id. at *6.

                                   3          By contrast, PVC Fence has offered no evidence that Google pressured advertisers not to

                                   4   opt out or otherwise made it difficult to opt out. PVC Fence asserts that Google did so by requiring

                                   5   advertisers to complete a “Sisyphean task” involving “multiple steps” to review the arbitration

                                   6   provision, which Google then presented in “a miniscule copy of the entirety of the Program

                                   7   Terms.” Yet those assertions are based on the allegations in PVC Fence’s unverified first amended

                                   8   complaint, which are not evidence. See Hansen, 1 F.4th at 670 (noting that a motion to compel

                                   9   arbitration is reviewed under the summary-judgment standard); Moran v. Selig, 447 F.3d 748,

                                  10   759–60 (9th Cir. 2006) (noting that neither an unverified complaint nor the parties’ opposition or

                                  11   reply briefs may be considered as evidence at the summary-judgment stage). And as detailed

                                  12   above, Google has offered substantial evidence that it provided unambiguous notice to advertisers
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   of their ability to opt out in multiple places, including at the top of the page on which Google

                                  14   required advertisers to accept the September 2017 terms.

                                  15          Accordingly, PVC Fence has not raised a genuine dispute as to the unconscionability of the

                                  16   arbitration provision, and it cannot avoid arbitration on that ground.

                                  17          B.      None of PVC Fence’s claims seek public injunctive relief
                                  18          PVC Fence also argues that its UCL and FAL claims cannot be compelled to arbitration

                                  19   because those claims seek public injunctive relief. Under the McGill rule, an agreement to waive

                                  20   the right to seek public injunctive relief in any forum, including arbitration, cannot be enforced as

                                  21   a matter of California law. See McGill v. Citibank, N.A., 2 Cal.5th 945, 956 (2017); see also Blair

                                  22   v. Rent-A-Ctr., Inc., 928 F.3d 819, 830–31 (9th Cir. 2019) (holding that the FAA does not preempt

                                  23   this rule). Google concedes that PVC Fence cannot pursue public relief in arbitration under the

                                  24   provision at issue here, but contends that PVC Fence does not seek any form of public injunctive

                                  25   relief subject to the McGill rule.

                                  26          As the Court has explained elsewhere, public injunctive relief “must have the primary

                                  27   purpose and effect of prohibiting unlawful acts that threaten future injury to the general public,

                                  28   cannot constitute the pursuit of representative claims or relief on behalf of others, and should
                                                                                          7
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP            Document 46          Filed 03/16/26     Page 8 of 10




                                   1   present diffuse benefits to the general public as a whole.” Crane III, 722 F. Supp. 3d at 1036

                                   2   (citing Hodges v. Comcast Cable Commc’ns, LLC, 21 F.4th 535, 541–42 (9th Cir. 2021)). Or as

                                   3   the Ninth Circuit has explained, such relief is “limited to forward-looking injunctions that seek to

                                   4   prevent future violations of law for the benefit of the general public as a whole, as opposed to a

                                   5   particular class of persons, and that do so without the need to consider the individual claims of any

                                   6   non-party.” Hodges, 21 F.4th at 544. So where relief would only benefit a group of defendant’s

                                   7   customers, or a particularly “discrete class of persons who are similarly situated to the plaintiff[],”

                                   8   it does not qualify as public injunctive relief. See id. at 545; see also McGill, 2 Cal.5th at 955

                                   9   (explaining that public injunctive relief “by and large benefits the general public” and “benefits the

                                  10   plaintiff, if at all, only incidentally and/or as a member of the general public” (citation modified)).

                                  11          Here, PVC Fence’s FAL and UCL claims do not seek diffuse benefits to the public as a

                                  12   whole—they seek to benefit plaintiff and other similarly situated (current or future) users of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Google Ads. For example, PVC Fence’s FAL claim “seek[s] restitution” and “injunctive relief …

                                  14   requiring Google to cease and desist from publishing false, deceptive, and misleading marketing

                                  15   statements related to the Google Ads product and service.” PVC Fence’s UCL claim similarly

                                  16   seeks “restitution” and “declaratory and injunctive relief” that would require Google to (1) “cease

                                  17   refusing to provide [PVC Fence] and [other] Google Ads users necessary information” concerning

                                  18   placement of their advertisements and (2) “cease making false claims in its advertising

                                  19   promulgated towards Google Ads users and potential users concerning the information it

                                  20   provides.” This requested relief would benefit only current and future Google Ads users, who

                                  21   allegedly suffer harm from Google’s failure to provide advertisement-placement information and

                                  22   its misrepresentations about the information it offers to advertisement purchasers.

                                  23          Where the California Supreme Court has held that injunctions prohibiting deceptive

                                  24   advertising practices amounted to public relief, however, the challenged practices were in markets

                                  25   in which nearly all individuals participate, such that the requested relief would necessarily benefit

                                  26   the public as a whole. See, e.g., McGill, 2 Cal.5th at 952, 956–57 (consumer credit market); Cruz

                                  27   v. PacifiCare Health Sys., Inc., 30 Cal. 4th 303, 315–16 (2003) (healthcare); Broughton v. Cigna

                                  28   Healthplans of Cal., 21 Cal. 4th 1066, 1072, 1080 (1999) (same). PVC Fence offers no evidence
                                                                                          8
                                        Case 5:25-cv-05480-PCP            Document 46         Filed 03/16/26     Page 9 of 10




                                   1   that most consumers participate in the advertisement-purchasing market, so there is no reason to

                                   2   conclude that relief directed to advertisement purchasers would provide an identifiable benefit to

                                   3   the general public.

                                   4          At the hearing on this matter, PVC Fence argued that its requested relief constitutes public

                                   5   injunctive relief because it will have positive downstream effects on the market as a whole. The

                                   6   Court has previously held that prospective relief with such market-wide effects may amount to a

                                   7   public injunction. See Crane III, 722 F.Supp.3d at 1036–37. But in Crane III, the Court did so in

                                   8   the face of specific arguments describing how the relief would result in such market-wide benefits.

                                   9   The plaintiff in that case explained that its requested injunction prohibiting monopolistic activity

                                  10   in the online-search market “would provide diffuse benefits to the public by potentially bolstering

                                  11   competition in the search and search advertising markets, increasing consumer choice, improving

                                  12   data privacy, and decreasing costs for both general search engine users and digital advertisers like”
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the plaintiff. Id. at 1036. And the plaintiff detailed how “[g]reater competition could” in turn

                                  14   “accelerate innovation, bringing positive downstream effects on internet users as a whole.” Id. at

                                  15   1036–37. PVC Fence has provided no such explanation here. Its speculative and general assertions

                                  16   of downstream market-wide effects are insufficient to transform the particularized relief it seeks

                                  17   into a public injunction.

                                  18           Because PVC Fence has not raised a genuine dispute about whether the arbitration

                                  19   provision is enforceable, either based on unconscionability or under the McGill rule, the Court

                                  20   must enforce the arbitration provision to the FAA. Google’s motion to compel arbitration is

                                  21   therefore granted.

                                  22   III.   Google’s motion to dismiss the first amended complaint is denied.
                                  23          In the alternative to its motion to compel arbitration, Google asks that the Court dismiss

                                  24   PVC Fence’s first amended complaint for lack of standing and failure to state a claim. Because the

                                  25   parties have agreed that an arbitrator, and not the Court, must address such merits issues, the

                                  26   alternative motion is denied without prejudice. Cf. Henry Schein, Inc. v. Archer & White Sales,

                                  27   Inc., 586 U.S. 63, 69 (2019) (explaining that “a court may not decide a merits question that the

                                  28   parties have delegated to an arbitrator”).
                                                                                         9

                                   1                                             CONCLUSION

                                   2          For the foregoing reasons, the Court denies Google’s motions to strike and to dismiss and

                                   3   grants its motion to compel arbitration. At Google’s request, the Court stays the proceedings in

                                   4   this case pending mediation or arbitration. See 9 U.S.C. § 3; Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472, 478

                                   5   (2024). By no later than March 1 and September 1 of each year, Google shall provide the Court

                                   6   with an update on the status of the arbitration proceedings.

                                   7          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                   8   Dated: March 16, 2026
